intro: A linear system is a set of equations that must all be true at once. This branch teaches a reliable, step-by-step method for solving any such system, however many unknowns it has.

VII.2.01.what: Writing a set of equations as a matrix, a rectangular table of numbers, so only the numbers that matter are kept.

levels.a: Writes the numbers in front of the unknowns as a table (the coefficient matrix).
levels.b: Adds the right-hand-side numbers as an extra column (the augmented matrix).
levels.c: Writes the whole system in the short form: matrix times unknowns equals answers.
levels.d: Writes the system as a combination of column vectors that must hit a target.

VII.2.02.what: Row operations are three safe moves on the rows of a matrix that simplify a system without changing its solutions.

levels.b: Multiplies a row by a nonzero number.
levels.c: Adds a multiple of one row to another row.
levels.d: Explains why these moves never gain or lose any solutions.

VII.2.03.what: Row echelon form is a staircase shape the matrix is tidied into, which makes the system easy to solve from the bottom up.

levels.a: Recognizes the staircase shape, with zeros below each step.
levels.b: Uses row operations to clear out numbers below each step, working downward.
levels.c: Identifies the pivots, the first nonzero number on each step.
levels.d: Solves from the bottom row up, substituting as it goes.

VII.2.04.what: Reduced row echelon form is the tidiest possible version of the matrix, where the answers can be read off directly.

levels.a: Scales rows so each pivot becomes a 1.
levels.b: Clears the numbers above each pivot to zero as well.
levels.c: Runs the full process from start to finish (Gauss–Jordan elimination).
levels.d: Understands that every matrix tidies to exactly one such final form.

VII.2.05.what: Unknowns that land on a pivot are fixed by the others; the rest (free variables) can be anything, which is how systems get infinitely many answers.

levels.a: Picks out the unknowns tied to pivots (the basic variables).
levels.b: Picks out the free variables, which can take any value.
levels.c: Decides whether a system has no solution, one, or infinitely many.
levels.d: Predicts the possible outcomes just from the matrix's shape.

VII.2.06.what: When there are infinitely many solutions, they can be described neatly by letting the free variables vary, like tracing all points along a line.

levels.a: Writes each basic variable in terms of the free ones.
levels.b: Writes the full solution as a fixed vector plus multiples of other vectors.
levels.c: Pictures the solution set as a point, line or plane.
levels.d: Checks that a proposed solution really satisfies every equation.

VII.2.07.what: A system is consistent if it has at least one solution. Some systems contradict themselves and have none.

levels.a: Spots a row that says 0 equals a nonzero number, meaning no solution.
levels.b: Decides whether a given system has any solution at all.
levels.c: Finds which right-hand-side values make a system solvable.
levels.d: Separates two questions: is there a solution, and is it the only one.

VII.2.08.what: A homogeneous system has every equation equal to zero. It always has the all-zeros solution, and sometimes many more.

levels.a: Recognizes and sets up a system where every right-hand side is zero.
levels.b: Notes that setting every unknown to zero always works.
levels.c: Decides when other, nonzero solutions exist too.
levels.d: Describes all the solutions as everything reachable from a few vectors.

VII.2.09.what: Linear systems model real problems with many interlocking quantities, from traffic on streets to chemistry to electronics.

levels.a: Sets up and solves traffic or pipe networks where flow in equals flow out.
levels.b: Balances chemical equations so atoms on both sides match.
levels.c: Finds currents in simple electrical circuits.
levels.d: Finds a smooth curve that passes exactly through given points.
